accuracy.evidence: Checked against Chemguide's alcohol pages and the AQA GCSE organic chemistry content: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH with CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH, C₄H₉OH; aqueous alcohols neutral (pH 7); sodium reacts more gently than with water giving H₂ and the alkoxide (2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂, and the alkoxide solution is alkaline, which the sandbox shows); combustion equations balanced by atom count for n = 1–4 (C₂H₅OH + 3O₂; 2CH₃OH + 3O₂; 2C₃H₇OH + 9O₂; C₄H₉OH + 6O₂); oxidation gives the carboxylic acid with the same carbons; fermentation of sugar by yeast. Methanol–propanol fully miscible, butanol partly.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the common GCSE slips: C₄H₁₀OH (keeping all the alkane H), believing –OH makes alcohols alkaline (taught by indicator next to NaOH), forgetting the alcohol's own O when balancing (3½O₂ for ethanol), counting O atoms instead of O₂ molecules, expecting CO₂ or no reaction with sodium, confusing burning with oxidation to an acid, and alkane/alkene names for the oxidation product.

lab_distinct.evidence: A dedicated alcohol bench with three linked views: a displayed-formula builder for methanol to butanol, test tubes where indicator, sodium and an oxidiser chips are dragged onto tubes (live pH colours and hydrogen bubbles), and a burner where O₂ molecules are dragged into a reactant box against a live C/H/O atom tally with a ×2 alcohol control. Nearest existing lab is the functional-groups lab; shingle overlap is low and it shares no pH, oxidation or balancing mechanic.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the learner do the chemistry: build the series and read 2n + 1, see green beside purple to break the –OH = alkali idea, compare sodium fizz in ethanol and water, balance ethanol by adding O₂ until the oxygen bars match, discover that methanol and propanol need doubling because O₂ comes in pairs, and watch pH fall from 7 to 3 as alcohols become acids.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions before the action, each with plausible wrong options taken from real slips (C₄H₁₀OH, purple because –OH, no reaction or CO₂ with sodium, 3½ or 7 for ethanol's O₂, ethene or only CO₂ and water on oxidation). The reveal names the learner's own choice and explains why it was wrong.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight generated challenge questions across formulas, O₂ counts, pH, gas from sodium, oxidation product and combustion products. Every wrong option maps to a named slip with targeted feedback, e.g. picking 13 for butanol explains that 13 O are in the products, the alcohol brings 1, so O₂ gives 12 O: 6 O₂. Verified by a real-pointer walk through all challenge questions.

readability.evidence: Learner explanation Flesch–Kincaid grade 4.7 (kid) and 7.4 (adult), within the 6.5 and 9.5 limits. Short sentences, one idea each, equations kept to the adult track and worked example; lab texts are one or two sentences per step.

no_filler.evidence: No filler phrases; every paragraph carries a fact, a reason or a named mistake. Explanation overlap with existing lessons 0–low, content gate passes, and the family tip is a concrete label-reading task tied to uses as fuels and solvents.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at Android dark, iPhone 13 light and desktop light for all eight steps: burner box was shortened so it no longer overlaps the atom-count legend, chips and tubes fit on a 390 px screen, and the phone sweep reports 0 findings. Real pointer drags on iPhone 13 complete the indicator, sodium and O₂ tasks.

accessibility.evidence: Canvas has a live aria-label describing tubes, pH colours, fizzing and atom balance; every drag has button equivalents (Indicator → 1, + O₂, − O₂, × 2 alcohol); controls are grouped with an aria-label; axe passes in dark and light themes with no console errors in the browser gate.
